text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer has responded to the High Court Wik decision, saying it is the government's responsibility to develop a national response to the native title problem, rather than hand the matter over to the states, which, he described, would be like playing "Pontius Pilate". Page 1.

An Australian Business Chamber survey of more than 500 manufacturing firms in New South Wales has found that an overhaul of the tax system would be the best way to restore business confidence. It has also revealed that the introduction of a consumption tax would be the best way to revitalise the sector for the up-coming year. Page 3.

A flood of cheap new cars onto the market has left used car dealers facing losses of tens of millions of dollars. The new car price war has not only seen used car sales reduced, but it has also undermined the value of used car stocks. Page 2.

Following Australian Conservation Foundation claims that Energy Resources of Australia was releasing contaminated low-grade water and other toxic material from the Ranger uranium mine into Kakadu National Park, the company was forced yesterday to deny any history of water management problems at the mine. Page 4.
THE AUSTRALIAN

The Howard Government has elected retired secondary school principal Roderick West to chair a review panel designed to draw-up a blueprint for higher education policy in the next 20 years, a move which paves the way for top-level examination of vouchers fr students and commercialisation of universities to an extent previously unheard of in Australia. Page 1.

Sources at two leading research universities - the University of Melbourne and at Australia's largest university, Monash - have confirmed the institutions may lower their entry scores for undergraduate science and engineering courses. This follows a sharp fall in student demand, thought to be due to the government's three-tiered Higher Education Contribution Scheme, which increases the relative cost of a science degree. Page 1.

In a move that bolsters recent calls from both the Victorian and South Australian premiers, Jeff Kennett and John Olsen, the housing, manufacturing, tourism and construction sectors, as well as peak employer groups, have joined the Business Council of Australia push for an overhaul of Australia's taxation system. Page 1.

Following claims from Darwin euthanasia doctor Philip Nitschke, the doctor of the first two patients to die under the Northern Territory's controversial euthanasia legislation, that another 40 people wish to use it, pressure has intensified on the Howard government to allow a rapid Senate vote on the bill to overturn the laws. Page 3.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Speaking after the release of the 1996 Higher School Certificate results, which showed inequities in the school system, with stark differences in performance between schools, New South Wales Premier Bob Carr told this year's HSC students yesterday they must "work harder than you have ever worked before" if they want to go to university. Page 1.

Yesterday announcing a A$40 million upgrade of Sydney's most famous thoroughfare, George Street, New South Wales Premier Bob Carr said the makeover of the street's southern end would be in time for the Olympic Games and would see it turned into a "boulevard-style street", in keeping with its position in the city's life. Page 1.

In a move which means five New South Wales Government departments are now left without permanent heads, the Health Department yesterday confirmed the resignation of its Director-General, John Wyn Owen, who is returning to Britain next month with more than two years of his five-year contract left to run. Page 1.

A study of vehicle emissions by the CSIRO's Division of Coal and Energy Technology indicates Sydney's peak hour has slowed to such a slow pace that motorists and their passengers are exposed to levels of benzene - a known carcinogen - up to 27 times that of normal levels when travelling in their cars. Page 3.
THE AGE

The rising stars of world tennis had a mixed opening day in the Australian Open in Melbourne yesterday. Day One saw crowd favourite Martina Hingis progress to the second round, but not so lucky was 15-year-old Lleyton Hewitt from Adelaide, who lost in straight sets. The day however was highlighted by the breakdown of Jennifer Capriati, who left her press conference in tears after losing to a lowly ranked player. Page A1.

Aboriginal groups in Victoria are considering adopting a radical approach to the High Court Wik decision by waiving their right to individual claims, in return for an agreement with the state government which would result in a better delivery of essential services. Page A1.

The Australian Olympic Committee looks set to lose an estimated A$7 million after risky speculation in the Reef Casino in Cairns. The Reef Casino units, which the IOC bought more than eight million of between 1993 and 1995, were suspended on the stock exchnge yesterday, as the casino battled to stave off receivership. Page A1.

Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett and his Police Minister Bill McGrath were in disagreement yesterday over the seriousness of a break in at the police drug squad, which saw files on one of the state's largest drug investigations stolen. The theft has also foced Kennett to dismiss allegations of corruption which have been levelled at the police force in recent days. Page A1.
